title: The strategy that gained 200 percent by being wrong way round

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Antoine ran a simple trading rule on hundreds of stocks and crypto pairs, and one coin came out with roughly two hundred percent return. Sounds great, until you see what buy-and-hold did on the same coin.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Let me guess. It lost a lot.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: About eighty percent. The rule didn't discover a secret. It happened to be short while the price collapsed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, back up. What's the rule?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's an EMA crossover. An EMA is a moving average that weighs recent prices more. When the twenty-period one crosses above the eighty-period one, the strategy buys. When it crosses back, it sells. Each trade has a ten percent stop loss and a twenty-five percent take profit.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And he ran that across a whole market?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, with a tool called BatchBacktesting. It pulls daily prices from Financial Modeling Prep for the S and P five hundred, or from Binance for crypto, runs the strategy on each ticker using backtesting dot py, and writes CSV results and optional charts. He ran it on twelve threads.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what did the leaderboard look like?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The top was Bitcoin against the BUSD stablecoin at plus two hundred ninety-four percent. The bottom was a token called BTT at minus ninety-nine point nine percent. And the stocks UAL and NCLH lost over eighty percent, because the COVID period punishes naive trend rules.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So you can't just buy the winners tomorrow.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Definitely not. Antoine says the top and bottom lists are diagnostics, not buy and sell lists. The best result is probably a rule fitted to that window, and the backtest ignores things like fees, slippage, and liquidity.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Seeing the distribution of outcomes under a simple rule. He calls it invaluable for humility and dangerous as autopilot. And always open the chart for a ticker before telling a story about it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A screening hammer, not a portfolio manager.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: His own words, nearly. The full write-up has the code, the leaderboard and the buy-and-hold comparison chart.
